Counting Chips On a Circle

InvariantsCountingParity
Game: Half the chips round the circle are red and half are green. However you arrange them, some half of the circle has as many red chips as green. Try to beat it!
How to play: Click a chip to change its colour. Keep the reds and greens equal, and watch the line that cuts the circle in half.

Reds minus greens on the half circle starting at each chip

Look for the math

Place 2n red and 2n green chips evenly round a circle. However they are arranged, some half circle (2n neighbouring chips) holds exactly n of each.

One step at a time

Let r(m) be the number of reds in the half circle that starts at chip m. Moving the start one chip on drops one chip and takes in the next, so r stays the same or changes by exactly 1. The graph under the circle shows r(m) − g(m) for every start: it moves in steps of 0 or 2.

The other half

The half circle starting at m + 2n is everything the half at m leaves out, so r(m + 2n) = 2n − r(m). If one half has fewer than n reds, the opposite half has more than n. Walking the start from m to m + 2n one step at a time, the count must pass through n exactly. This is a discrete intermediate value theorem: the graph crosses zero, and it does so in opposite pairs.

Checked

The logic test tried every arrangement of equal reds and greens for 4 to 20 chips, more than 200,000 in all, and found a balanced half every time. It also checked both facts the proof uses. With unequal numbers the claim can fail: a circle of all red chips has no balanced half.

Group all the reds together. Where does the dividing line go now, and how many places could it go?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
